card.keepWhy: Meant for harm. Turned to good.
sources: Genesis 37:3-4 (Israel, i.e. Jacob, loved Joseph more than his other sons; made him a long coat, traditionally “coat of many colors”; his brothers hated him)
Genesis 37:26-28 (sold to Ishmaelite and Midianite traders for twenty pieces of silver, taken to Egypt)
Genesis 37:31-33 (they sent the coat to their father; Jacob concluded a wild animal had devoured him)
Genesis 39-41 (slavery in Potiphar’s house, prison, Pharaoh’s dreams); Genesis 41:40-41 (set over all the land of Egypt, second only to Pharaoh); 41:48-49, 56 (in charge of the grain)
Genesis 42:3, 6-8 (ten brothers come to buy grain, bow down to him with their faces to the earth; they did not recognize him)
Genesis 45:1-2 (he could not restrain himself; wept aloud, and the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard)
Genesis 45:4-5 (“I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt. Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves… God sent me before you to preserve life”)
Genesis 50:15-21 (after Jacob’s death the brothers fear revenge; Joseph weeps; “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good”; he comforted them and spoke kindly to them)
Matthew 6:12 (“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”), behind the today step’s prayer line, in its familiar liturgical form
check: The lesson skips Joseph’s long testing of his brothers (Genesis 42-44: the spy charge, Simeon held, Benjamin and the cup) and goes from the bowing to the reveal with “in time.” Confirm the shortening is fair.
The coat: Hebrew ketonet passim, traditionally “many colors,” possibly “long-sleeved.” The lesson says “richly colored.” Confirm.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there a hurt from your own family, or an old friend, that still stings?
options: i’m sorry. you don’t have to fix it today. just listen to this one.
that takes honesty to say. keep them in mind as you listen.
good. this story might help someone you love.

steps.line: Jacob loved his son Joseph most, and gave him a richly colored coat. Joseph’s older brothers hated him for it.
steps.label: Genesis 37:3-4

steps.line: So they sold him to traders headed for Egypt, and let their father believe a wild animal had killed him.
steps.label: Genesis 37:28-33

steps.q: Joseph arrives in Egypt as a slave. What do you think becomes of him?
o: He rises to help rule Egypt
He stays a slave all his life
steps.why: Through slavery and even prison, he rises, all the way to Pharaoh’s side.

steps.line: Through slavery and prison, Joseph rose until Pharaoh put him in charge of all Egypt and its grain, second only to the king.
steps.label: Genesis 41:40

steps.line: When famine struck, his brothers came to Egypt to buy food. They bowed low before him. They didn’t recognize him.
steps.label: Genesis 42:6-8

steps.q: You’re Joseph. The brothers who sold you are bowing, and they don’t know you. What does Joseph do first?
o: Tells them at once who he is
Sends them home with grain, saying nothing
steps.why: He speaks harshly and tests them for a long time. Many readers think he needed to know if they’d changed. When Judah offers himself in Benjamin’s place, Joseph breaks.

steps.line: In time, Joseph couldn’t hold back. He wept so loudly the whole palace heard. “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt.”
steps.label: Genesis 45:1-4

steps.q: The brother they sold is now the second most powerful man in Egypt. How do you think they react?
o: They deny they ever sold him
steps.why: Genesis says they couldn’t answer him. The boy they got rid of now held their lives in his hands.

steps.line: His brothers were too terrified to answer. He said, “Don’t be upset or angry with yourselves. God sent me ahead of you to save lives.”
steps.label: Genesis 45:3-5

steps.q: Joseph had every reason for revenge. What helped him forgive?
o: He saw God at work, even through the harm
Years had made him forget the hurt
He needed his brothers’ help in Egypt
steps.why: He hadn’t forgotten: “whom you sold,” he says. But he could see God bringing life out of it.

steps.pre: After their father died, the brothers feared revenge. Joseph wept: “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of
steps.why: Genesis 50:19. Revenge would mean playing judge, and Joseph refuses the role. Judging belongs to God.

steps.line: Years later, after their father died, the brothers feared revenge. Joseph wept again. “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”
steps.label: Genesis 50:15-20

say: here’s what i love. joseph never says it didn’t hurt. he names it: “you meant evil.” and he forgives anyway.
in jewish and christian tradition alike, his story is forgiveness held up by trust: the worst thing done to you doesn’t get the last word. God does.

steps.q: Joseph says, “God meant it for good.” Does that mean what his brothers did was okay?
o: Yes. It worked out, so no harm done
No. And he still planned to punish them
No. He calls it evil, and lets revenge go
steps.why: Forgiving isn’t pretending. Joseph names the wrong for what it was, and still lets go of revenge.

today.say: think of one old hurt you still carry. you don’t have to pretend it was okay. joseph didn’t. try saying it honestly, “that was wrong, and i’m letting go of getting even.” if you’d like, add the old prayer line, “forgive us, as we forgive”: watch, learn, or join in. your choice.
options: then you’ve already started. naming it is what joseph did first.
that’s okay. it took joseph years. you can start small.
